principles.name: Knowing your customer
principles.description: Understand the people who use the Terminal, news and data products, how they work under time pressure, and build what actually helps them make decisions.
evidence_signals: Names a specific user (trader, analyst, journalist, internal team) and their workflow
Gathered feedback from users directly instead of guessing
Measured the result in terms the user cares about, such as latency, accuracy or time saved

principles.name: Innovation
principles.description: Keep improving products and engineering practice: new data sets, new tools and better ways of building, while keeping a long-lived product reliable.
evidence_signals: Proposed and built a new approach instead of patching around a problem
Modernized legacy code or infrastructure without breaking users
Shows curiosity about technology and finance beyond the task

principles.name: Collaboration
principles.description: Work across teams and functions, share knowledge openly and help colleagues succeed.
evidence_signals: Worked with another team, product or data group to ship a result
Resolved a disagreement with a teammate by listening and finding common ground
Credits others with 'we' and owns own part with 'I'

principles.name: Doing the right thing
principles.description: Act with integrity toward clients, colleagues and communities: accurate data, honest communication and responsibility for mistakes.
evidence_signals: Raised a data-quality or correctness problem even when it was inconvenient
Admitted a mistake early and fixed it
Puts accuracy and trust ahead of shipping fast

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, resume and a real 'why Bloomberg' check. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical phone screen
rounds.notes: One or two live coding rounds on HackerRank CodePair, LeetCode-medium level, often with a constraint added midway. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Onsite coding
rounds.notes: One or two harder data-structures rounds (graphs, trees, intervals, streams). Interviewers give hints. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: Real-time financial systems: market data distribution, alerting, news pipelines, Terminal-scale services. Follow-ups ask what fails first and how you would know. Lighter or object-oriented design for entry-level candidates.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: Often the most technical conversation: deep dive into resume projects, language trade-offs (C++, Python, Java), plus team fit and motivation.

rounds.name: HR close
rounds.notes: Culture fit, teamwork and conflict questions, why Bloomberg, logistics.

rounds.name: Coding
rounds.notes: Live coding similar to the SWE loop. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: ML and NLP deep dive
rounds.notes: Past ML projects and applied problems close to Bloomberg's products, such as real-time news NLP, entity tagging and sentiment signals for the Terminal.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: Product experience and why Bloomberg; candidates report being told to expect a case at this stage.

rounds.name: Product case
rounds.notes: Terminal or data-product problem for a professional user, such as helping analysts spot trends. Some teams ask for a short presentation of how the candidate solved a past product problem.

rounds.name: Behavioral
rounds.notes: Working with engineers and clients; evidence-based decisions.

question_patterns.pattern: Why the candidate wants Bloomberg specifically, tied to its products, users or engineering work
A disagreement with a teammate about an approach and how it was resolved
A time the candidate found a data or correctness problem and had to decide whether to ship
Walk through one project on the resume: design, own role, trade-offs and what would change now
Compare languages or tools the candidate has used and when each fits
Design a low-latency system that ingests and distributes financial data or news to many users
For a design, what fails first under load and how the team would detect and recover
Model the classes and data flow for a small system that processes and stores user data
Design or improve a Terminal-style feature for a specific finance user, with a success metric

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a conflict you had with a teammate and how you handled it.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real technical or priority disagreement, not a personality clash. Explain both positions fairly, how you listened and used evidence (a benchmark, data, a user need) to converge, and what was decided. Show the relationship stayed good and what you learned about working with that person. Pitfalls: making the other person the villain, or a conflict that resolved itself.

looking_for: How you handle disagreement with peers
Whether you use evidence rather than authority
strong_signals: Converges with data or a test

sample_questions.question: Which experience on your resume best prepared you for this role, and why?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Choose one experience and connect it to what Bloomberg engineers do: performance-sensitive code, data correctness, serving demanding users. Give the problem, your specific contribution, a measurable result, and the skill you took away. Pitfalls: listing everything, or picking something with no link to the role.

sample_questions.question: Why do you want to work at Bloomberg rather than a big tech company or a bank?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Show real knowledge: the Terminal and its professional users, the mix of finance, news and data, the scale of real-time data, open-source work, or the philanthropy model. Tie it to your own interests and past work. A strong answer is specific enough that it could not be said about any other company. Pitfalls: generic praise, or focusing on pay.

looking_for: Understanding of its products and users
strong_signals: Names specific products or engineering work

sample_questions.question: Design a system that delivers real-time market price updates to thousands of Terminal users with low latency.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify scale (instruments, update rate, subscribers) and latency goals. Propose ingestion from exchanges, normalization, a publish-subscribe fan-out layer, per-client subscription filtering and conflation for slow consumers. Discuss ordering, gaps and recovery (sequence numbers, snapshots plus deltas), failover across data centers, and monitoring for staleness. Explain trade-offs such as push versus pull and conflation versus completeness.

watch_outs: One big database as the answer

sample_questions.question: Design an alerting service that notifies users when a price or news condition they set is met.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define alert types and scale, then separate rule storage, a streaming evaluator partitioned by instrument, deduplication and delivery channels. Cover exactly-once versus at-least-once delivery, avoiding alert storms, latency targets and what happens when the evaluator falls behind. Explain how you would know it is broken: lag metrics and synthetic alerts.

sample_questions.question: Pick a project from your resume and walk me through the design decisions you made and what you would do differently.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give context in a minute, then go deep: the requirements, the main design choice, the alternative you rejected and why, how you tested it, and what broke in production. Be precise about your own part. End with a concrete change you would make now. Pitfalls: staying high level, or not being able to answer follow-ups about details.

sample_questions.question: How would you build a system that tags breaking news stories with the companies they mention and a sentiment signal, in near real time?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify latency and accuracy needs. Cover the pipeline: ingestion, entity recognition and linking to a company identifier, sentiment or impact scoring, and publishing to users. Discuss model choice versus latency, ambiguous names, labeled data and evaluation (precision matters more than recall for a trading signal), monitoring for drift, and a human review path for errors.

sample_questions.question: Design a feature that helps equity analysts spot emerging market trends faster.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick one analyst segment and their current workflow, find the slowest or noisiest step, and propose one focused feature using Bloomberg's data and news. Define success (time to insight, adoption, retention) and how you would test it with real users. Prioritize, name what you would not build first, and note data-quality risks.

watch_outs: A long feature list with no priority

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Delivers well-defined features in one team with guidance; strong data structures and one object-oriented language.
Owns features end to end within a team and works directly with product and users.
Leads the technical direction of a team's systems, mentors junior engineers and designs for performance and reliability.
Leads a team of engineers, sets its technical roadmap and coordinates with other teams; usually also hands-on.

persona.pace: Moderate; adds a new constraint midway and gives hints when the candidate stalls
persona.pushback_style: Asks 'why this choice?', 'what fails first?', 'how would you know it broke?' and probes details of the candidate's own projects
persona.closing_style: Leaves time for the candidate's questions and expects real interest in Bloomberg

case_style.notes: PM cases start from a professional finance user (analyst, trader, journalist) and the Terminal's data and news. Engineering 'cases' are real-time data system designs. Market sizing is rare.

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: the four values come from job-board profiles (JobTeaser, Built In); Bloomberg's own careers and interview-guide pages returned 403, so exact wording ('Knowing your customer' versus 'customer service') is unconfirmed. Descriptions and evidence signals are our own.
loop_structure: SWE rounds come from two prep sites and agree well; data_ml and pm loops rest on thin candidate reports and prep blogs, and list no levels.

bar_by_level: Bloomberg has two IC titles (Software Engineer, Senior Software Engineer); the entry versus mid split inside 'Software Engineer' and mapping Team Lead to staff_principal are our judgment. Team Lead is a manager role.
persona: inferred from prep-site descriptions of hints, added constraints and design follow-ups.
scoring_weights: our estimate; 'why Bloomberg' motivation is reported as able to sink an offer, so motivation is raised.
case_style: PM case examples come from prep sites partly behind paywalls; we used only the publicly visible prompt themes.
